activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus; the cell wall in plants lies outside the membrane rather than replacing it.
story:
Sophia pressed her nose close to the giant model of a plant cell, then crossed the hall to the model of an animal cell beside it. Her worksheet had one question left, and it was the one Blair had dared her to answer without help: name the parts that only plant cells have.

"Easy," Sophia had said at school. "Plants have that wall thing, and animals don't."

"Fine," Blair had said. "But Mr. Rajapakse said half the class got that question wrong last year. He said people make the same mistake every time."

Now, at the museum, Sophia stared at the plant cell model. There was the thick outer wall, green and bumpy. Inside it, drawn as a second layer, was a thinner skin. She frowned. If plants had a wall, why would they also need that inner layer?

She walked back to the animal cell and traced its outside with her finger. The same thin skin, no wall around it. Frances appeared beside her, holding a translucent plastic sheet printed with cell diagrams from the gift shop. "Look," Frances said, "they printed the labels on this. The conductor of the tour said we could borrow one."

Sophia laid the sheet over the plant cell model and adjusted it until the lines matched. Both models had a label on the thin skin. "Cell membrane," she read. The wall lay outside it, like a coat worn over a jacket.

"So the wall doesn't replace the membrane," Sophia said slowly. "It's extra."

"And both cells have the membrane," Frances said, "plus the cytoplasm inside, and the nucleus. I found all three labels on both models."

Sophia copied the parts onto her worksheet: membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus in both; then, under "plant cells only," she wrote the cell wall, and after spotting the green ovals in the plant model but not the animal one, she added chloroplasts for good measure.

At school the next day, Mr. Rajapakse handed the worksheets back. He paused at Sophia's page and raised his eyebrows. "Half the class wrote that plants traded their membrane for a wall," he said. "You didn't."

Sophia grinned and slid the page into her folder, right behind the translucent sheet, which she had decided to keep.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens.
story:
Peyton had signed up for the geology club on a whim, mostly because her friend Carina had enrolled first and had promised there would be snacks. There were no snacks. There was a long table in the science room covered with numbered rocks, and Mr. Girma's instruction on the board: sort them into igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic. Each basket held one kind, and each rock had a small card telling where it had been found, nothing more.

Peyton picked up rock number seven, which was speckled black and gray, like somebody had spilled two colors of paint and forgotten to stir. Carina leaned over. "That one's giving me despair," she said. "It looks like every other rock."

"It doesn't, though," Peyton said slowly. "Look at the speckles. They're all over, inside it, not just on the outside." Rock number twelve, which she had already put in the sedimentary basket, had layers, like a stack of old pancakes. She had reasoned that something with layers had probably been built up bit by bit. But speckles weren't layers. Speckles looked like things that had been mixed together and then frozen in place.

"I think this one was melted," she said. "Like, actually melted, all runny, and then it got hard again, and the speckles got stuck wherever they were." She turned the rock over. The speckles went all the way through. If it had only been painted or rubbed, they would stop at the surface. That was her test, and the rock passed it.

Mr. Girma wandered past her table. Peyton held it up. "Was this ever melted? Like lava?"

"Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens," he said, which was not exactly a yes, but was close enough. He dropped one small piece of chalk into her basket as a point.

Behind her, Gabryel was still holding a gray lump over the desolate empty metamorphic basket, looking like a kid who had enrolled in the wrong club entirely. Peyton slid rock number seven into igneous, then walked over and picked up the gray lump. It had stripes that bent, like playdough that had been squished while soft.

"Everything gets squished and cooked," she said. "You just have to figure out squished by what."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: More than 200 different viruses can cause the common cold, and rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause.
story:
Sofia sat propped against her pillows with a box of tissues and a thermometer she no longer trusted, because it had said 98.9 three times in a row while her head still pounded. Her cold was being obstinate; four days home from school and her nose refused to cooperate. On her laptop she had eleven tabs open, and in the group chat, Karim had just messaged: "You gave this to me and Sameer, we're both sick now. Thanks a lot."

She stared at the message. Karim was sneezing constantly. Sameer, who had replied with a string of miserable emojis, said his throat felt like sandpaper. Sofia's own throat had barely hurt at all. She typed: "Wait, we might not even have the same thing." Then she went looking, because it seemed strange that one bug could act so different in three people.

The first result made her sit up straight. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold, and rhinoviruses were the most frequent cause. "Rhinoviruses," she said out loud to the empty bedroom, testing the word. Two hundred. That explained why there was no one shot you could get in October and forget about colds until spring; it wasn't one enemy, it was a crowd. Which meant Karim blaming her was only maybe half right. They could have caught separate infections from three different sources, or hers could have mutated as it passed along, or, most likely, all three of them had picked up whatever was circulating through the whole sixth grade after the field trip.

She texted her findings, and for ten minutes the chat was pure argument. Karim insisted the timing proved it. Sameer said timing proved nothing because everyone on the bus had been coughing. Finally Sofia delegated the verdict to the only available expert: she emailed Ms. Nguyen, their science teacher, asking whether three people with three different sets of symptoms could all be said to have "a cold."

The reply came an hour later. "Short answer: yes. Longer answer: bring it up in class when you're back. It's a good question." Sofia grinned, screenshotted it into the chat, and wrote, "You owe me an apology AND a get-well smoothie." Below her message, three dots appeared, then disappeared, then appeared again.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: The site: operator limits a search to one website or domain ending, so adding site:.gov shows only pages from US government websites.
story:
The morning announcements had promised a storm, and everyone in the computer lab was arguing about whether school would close early. Harrison wanted the real answer, not rumors. When he typed "big storm tomorrow" into the search bar, the first result shouted "STORM SHUTS DOWN SCHOOLS?" in giant letters, with a button that said CLICK HERE. "That's an ad," said Malia, leaning over from the next computer. "It just wants you to click it. Real results don't yell at you." Harrison noticed the tiny word "Ad" tucked in the corner, almost invisible against the bright box. He scrolled past it.

The next results were worse. One site said snow, another said rain, and a third claimed the storm had "dissolved out to sea," though it didn't say how it knew. Malia's cousin had texted her that morning that school was definitely closing, and now Malia was texting everyone in her class. Harrison didn't want her spreading something wrong. "Let's find the actual warning," he said. "The real one, from the weather people."

He tried "storm warning," but a weather blog came up first, then a store selling flashlights, then a page so crowded with pop-ups that Malia made a face like she'd bitten a lemon. "This is like a junk drawer," she said. Harrison stared at the search box. There had to be a way to say, show me only the official pages. He remembered a poster Ms. Schneider had hung above the whiteboard, listing sites you could trust, and nearly every one ended in .gov.

Carefully, he typed: storm warning site:.gov. "What's the site part do?" Malia asked, scooting her chair over, its wheels making diagonal tracks across the floor. "Ms. Schneider says the site: operator limits a search to one website or domain ending," Harrison said. "So site:.gov shows only pages from US government websites." He hit enter, and the junk drawer vanished. The first result was the National Weather Service, plain and gray, no shouting, no buttons. It said a winter storm warning was in effect until tomorrow evening.

"It doesn't say anything about school," Malia said slowly, reading over his shoulder. "It just says heavy snow starting at six." They looked at each other. Then Malia picked up her phone and typed a quick message: "Wait, don't tell everyone yet. The warning runs till tomorrow night, so maybe school is open. Check the district page." She set the phone face down and pulled out a sheet of paper, drawing two boxes at the top. "Okay," she said, tapping the first box. "Write AD in this one. Help me sort the rest."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords: using only lowercase letters, adding one more letter makes 26 times as many possibilities to guess.
story:
Lincoln slid his library card across the desk and waited while Mr. Das checked out a fantasy novel with a dragon on the cover. At the computer stations behind the desk, Keaton was typing fast, then typing again, then slumping in his chair. "It kicked me out," Keaton said. "Third time. I made this password last month and it was great. Six letters. Bam. Nobody guesses that."

Lincoln sat down at the next computer and pulled a pencil from his backpack. Six letters sounded fine to him too, but Keaton was locked out, so something was wrong somewhere. On the back of a due-date slip he wrote the alphabet and counted the letters. Twenty-six. A one-letter password, all lowercase, had twenty-six possibilities. If you added a second letter, each first letter could pair with any of twenty-six second letters. He multiplied: 676. He kept going, and by the sixth letter the number ran off the slip and onto the table. The digits looked like a phone number for a whole city. "Every extra letter multiplies it," Lincoln said, more to himself than to Keaton.

"That doesn't mean mine's weak," Keaton said. "It's my dog's name plus my birthday, and nobody knows my dog." Then he frowned. "Except I used the same one for the game site. And the forum. And the pizza place."

Mr. Das leaned over the desk without leaving his stool. "Same password everywhere?"

"It's just one thing to remember," Keaton said.

Lincoln thought about that while the heater rattled and someone's printer groaned through a school report. One password was like one key for every door in town, and once somebody got a copy of it from the cheapest, weakest door, all the other doors opened too. The pizza site didn't need to be a fortress for Keaton's game account to fall. That was the part you couldn't see, the hidden chain. His fantasy novel waited in his lap, its protagonist facing a similar problem, one secret tunnel under all the castle walls at once.

"Try this," Lincoln said, and tore the slip in half. He wrote six random letters, then three more. "Nine letters instead of six. That's twenty-six times as many possibilities for every single one you add, so guessing gets huge, fast. And use a different one for the game site. Write them down at home until you remember them."

Keaton typed the new password, and the library catalog opened on his screen. He stared at it, then grinned and held up the torn slip. "You realize my dog is going to be furious at you for this."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
story:
The arena smelled like cold rubber and burnt coffee, and Hunter's breath made little clouds whenever he cheered. He was squeezed onto the bleachers between his dad and Iver, with Grady one row down, all of them watching the championship game. The home team was down by two with three minutes left, and every slam of the puck into the boards made the whole section jump.

During the timeout, the scoreboard screen flashed a trivia question for a free hot chocolate: WHO INVENTED BASKETBALL? Hunter frowned. Basketball? At a hockey game? "Easy," said Grady, turning around. "Some college guys, right? Like, in the nineteen twenties." Iver shook his head. "I think it was way earlier. And I bet it wasn't at a college. Why would a hockey rink ask that?"

Hunter started reasoning it through. "They wouldn't ask it here unless it connected somehow," he said slowly. "Indoor games, winter, getting invented all around the same kind of place. Gyms. Maybe a YMCA." Grady rolled his eyes, but Hunter kept going. "And if it started indoors in a gym, they'd need something to shoot into. Something easy to find." He pictured a gym in the eighteen hundreds, no nets anywhere, and an idea condensed into a single clear picture: baskets. Fruit baskets. "I bet they literally used baskets. Peach baskets, even. And some teacher invented it, not students." Grady snorted. "Fine. Hot chocolate says you're wrong. Loser buys." They shook on it, and Hunter's stomach tightened, because two dollars was significant money when you'd only brought five.

The home team scored twice in the final minute to win, and the whole section roared. Hunter hugged Iver so hard he knocked his dad's glove off the bleachers, and Grady's little sister, who had been shivering beside him, got wrapped in Grady's spare scarf without anyone saying a word about it.

Then the announcer read the answer over the loudspeaker, and the words scrolled across the big screen: JAMES NAISMITH INVENTED BASKETBALL IN DECEMBER 1891 AT A YMCA TRAINING SCHOOL IN SPRINGFIELD, MASSACHUSETTS, USING PEACH BASKETS AS THE GOALS. Hunter grabbed Iver's sleeve. "Peach baskets! I said peach baskets!" Grady stared at the screen, then down at his wallet, and his face went from despair to a grin in about two seconds. "A teacher. At a YMCA. In Massachusetts." He dug out his crumpled bills. "Man. I was so sure."

They stood in the hot chocolate line together, and Grady bought an extra cup for his sister without being asked, warming it between his mittens on the walk back. Iver leaned over to Hunter and said, "You actually thought that through instead of guessing. That was cool." Hunter sipped his cocoa, watched the Zamboni glide across the melting ice below, and smiled. "Next timeout, I'm betting my five dollars."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
story:
The classroom spelling bee started right after lunch, and Theo made it through six rounds before Mr. Ma read out the next word for him. "Your word is vaccine."

Theo knew that one. He pictured the poster in the nurse's office and spelled it without trouble. Jolene got "random" and missed it, adding an extra d, so she sat down in the front row beside Everly, who had been knocked out in round four by "document." Now it was Theo against a kid from the other fifth-grade class, and only one of them would go to the regional bee.

The other kid went out on "chandelier." Then Mr. Ma looked at his list and said, "Your word is treacle."

Theo's mind went blank. He had never seen that word. If he started guessing letters, he was finished, because once you said a letter you could not take it back. He stared at the ceiling tiles and tried to think. What could he do besides start spelling?

He remembered the sheet the regional bee had sent home in the fall. Spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it. He had skimmed it once and stuffed it in his backpack, and he had thought it was boring at the time. Now it did not seem boring at all.

"Can I have the definition?" he asked.

"A thick syrup," Mr. Ma said.

"Can I have the language of origin?"

"French."

"Can I have it in a sentence?"

"The pancakes were drowned in treacle."

French. Theo thought about the French words he knew. They often had silent endings, like "tableau" and "bureau." The word ended in a "cle" sound, but French spellings liked "le" at the end. There was no vowel in there, probably no extra syllable. T-r-e-a-c-l-e. His mouth was dry when he said the letters, one at a time.

"That is correct," Mr. Ma said. "Which makes Theo our classroom champion."

Jolene stood up and applauded so hard she knocked her chair sideways. Everly caught it and held it steady, still clapping with one hand. Theo walked back to his desk, and Mr. Ma held out the registration form for the regional bee.

"You'll want your parent to sign this tonight," he said. "And this time, actually read the rules sheet."

Theo folded it in half and put it in his front pocket, not his backpack.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
story:
Keira slid into her seat at the Science Club table just as Mr. Kapoor dimmed the lights. She had wanted all week to be the one to run the memory experiment, the one with the video of two cars and the different questions, and today was finally her turn. The room smelled of dry-erase markers and the burnt coffee from the teachers' lounge down the hall.

First she played the clip for Aariz. "How fast were the cars going when they hit each other?" she asked, reading from her card. Aariz squinted at the screen, tapping his pencil. "Maybe twenty-five miles an hour?" Next came Selena, who watched the exact same clip in the stuffy back corner of the room. Keira changed only one word. "How fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?" Selena didn't even pause. "Forty. At least forty."

Keira wrote both numbers in her notebook, then wrote them again. Same video, same speed, and the answers contradicted each other by fifteen miles an hour. The only difference was hit versus smashed. She wondered about her dad asking her last month whether Marcus had "smashed" into her in the crowded hallway, and how huge and mean the collision had seemed in her memory afterward, even though Marcus had apologized twice and his backpack had barely grazed her. Maybe the word had done that. Maybe her memory wasn't a recording at all.

She pulled out the science magazine Mr. Kapoor had left on the table and flipped until she found it: a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer. People who were asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that hit. She read it three times, her sneakers bouncing under the chair. "It's real," she said out loud. "It happened to me and it's real."

At the end of club, Mr. Kapoor asked who wanted to present at the science fair, and Keira's hand shot up before she had finished deciding. Her stamina for this project, she told Selena on the bus, would last months if it had to, and it wouldn't be vain to plan a big display, not if the idea was true. That night she texted Marcus: hey, that hallway thing wasn't as bad as I made it sound. Wanna run the video for my experiment? His reply came fast: "sure. but I get to ask the questions."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Fractures of the radius near the wrist are the most common fractures seen in children, and they usually happen from falling onto an outstretched hand.
story:
Mila sat in the back seat with her cast propped on a pillow, watching the hospital shrink in the side mirror. Her wrist ached inside the hard white shell, and the doctor's words kept turning over in her head. She had broken a bone called the radius, right near the wrist, and the doctor had said it was the most common broken bone in kids, period.

"I still don't get it," her dad said from the driver's seat. "You said you didn't even fall that hard."

That was the part that bothered Mila too. She remembered running for the bus, then lying on the sidewalk with her palm stinging. There was a blank in between. She tried to reconstruct it, the way Ms. Singh had shown them for science: observe, then formulate a guess you can actually check. Maybe she hadn't landed on her knees or her side. Maybe she had done the thing almost everybody does when they're about to fall, which is throw a hand out to catch themselves.

She pulled out her phone with her good arm and texted Angelo, who had broken his wrist last year. Did you fall on your hand? He answered fast: yeah, stuck my arm out on the stairs. Then she texted King, who had a cast in third grade from the monkey bars. His answer said the same thing: tried to grab the bar, missed, landed on my hand.

Both of them. It seemed almost bizarre that the same move could produce the same injury twice in kids she knew, but the pattern was there, and it matched what the doctor had said. It wasn't the falling that broke the wrist, she thought. It was the catching.

Her dad glanced at her in the mirror. "You look like you solved something."

"Sort of," Mila said. "Next time I fall, I'm not using my hand."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
At dinner Isabella pushed her rice around her plate and waited for the right moment. "The orange crackers," she said finally. "The ones we always get. Where are they?"

Her mother set down her fork. "They're four dollars a box now. Last month they were two. I bought the square ones instead." She nodded at the box on the counter, one Isabella had refused to even open after school.

"They smell weird," Isabella said. She picked one up, turned it over, and took a cautious bite. It cracked loudly. Actually it tasted nearly the same, salty and a little like toasted cheese. She ate three more before she admitted it, out loud, in a small voice: "Okay. They're fine."

At school the next day, her whole plan seemed to revolve around that box. She cornered Lionel by the water fountain and Mina at lunch, and she asked both of them the same question: "What crackers did your family buy this week?" Lionel held up a bag of the square kind, the exact brand from her counter. Mina pulled out the same brand in her lunch, and then, when Isabella stared, she said, "My mom says everyone's buying them now. The store shelf was almost empty Monday."

That was the piece Isabella had been missing. At home she had written her question on a napkin the night before: if the orange crackers cost more, where would the crackers people buy go? The answer hadn't been visible anywhere, but now she could see it in three shopping bags. "It's like a substitute," she told Mina, "the same job, different box." She even borrowed Mina's phone and checked the store's website, which listed the square crackers with a little tag that said "high demand."

That evening, she slid a sheet of paper across the dinner table before the plates were even cleared. At the top it read, in careful handwriting, "Question for the store." Below it: how many boxes of square crackers did they sell last month, and this month? Her father laughed and said the manager might not share that, and her mother warned that the store was probably too busy to answer a letter from a sixth grader, that a question like theirs could feel vulnerable to being ignored.

"Then I'll ask three times," Isabella said. She folded the paper, put it in her backpack, and set the box of square crackers in the middle of the table, right where everyone could reach it.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of something rises, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
Grandma lived one street away from the Saturday farmers' market, which Alexia considered the best thing about her house besides the drawer of stale candy. This morning Grandma handed her a tote bag and said, "Strawberries, please. Whatever they cost." At the first stand, a pint was four dollars and the line stretched past the honey table. At the second stand, a painted sign read EIGHT DOLLARS, and the space in front of it was completely desolate, except for one wasp.

Alexia dragged her friend Samira over by the sleeve. "Look. Same strawberries. One stand has a line to the fence, and this one has a wasp."

Samira squinted. "The wasp doesn't count as a customer."

"Nobody's buying the eight-dollar ones," Alexia said. "And in winter, Grandma pays even more than eight, and she still buys them, but she complains the whole time." She turned the idea over like a stone. "When the price goes up, people buy less. In summer everybody sells strawberries, so they're cheap and everybody buys a lot."

Alexia decided to test it. She marched up to the eight-dollar farmer and said, "Sir, if you lowered your price, would all those people in that line come over here?"

The farmer scratched his chin. "Some would. That's the law of demand. When the price rises, people buy less, as long as nothing else changes."

"Nothing else," Alexia repeated, like she was laying a foundation for something. She looked sideways at the line. "Unless your strawberries are secretly magic."

"They're not magic," the farmer said. "They're just greedy strawberries."

Back at Grandma's kitchen table, Alexia spread out her finds: one four-dollar pint, one notebook, and a plan to write it all down for Monday's class, since Ms. Fortin had asked for a real-world example and Alexia intended to prioritize strawberries over everything else she could have picked. Charles-Olivier had suggested writing about video games. Video games. He was going to be so jealous of her wasp.

Alexia bit into a strawberry and drew a chart with two prices and two lines, one thick, one empty.

"This," she told Samira, "is going to be the best presentation in the history of presentations."

Samira stole a strawberry and said, "In the history of strawberries."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food such as milk should not sit out for more than two hours, or one hour above 32 degrees Celsius.
story:
Jade counted the money twice before she left home: one five, three ones, and a quarter for the bubble gum she was not going to buy. Her mother had said she was ready, and Jade wanted to prove it. The store was only four blocks away, but today the sun hammered the sidewalk, and by the time she reached the dairy case her shirt was sticking to her back. While she hunted for the latest date on the milk cartons, she reread the sign taped to the cooler door, the one she'd noticed on every trip with her dad but never really looked at. It said perishable food like milk should not sit out for more than two hours, or more than one hour when it was above 32 degrees Celsius outside. She'd always thought signs like that were background noise, part of the store's ecosystem of warnings, like wet floor signs and no smoking signs. Now she filed it away.

The cashier rang her up and Jade did the subtraction in her head before he said the total. "That's milk at three seventy-nine, out of six," she said, and he nodded and counted her change into her palm. She checked it coin by coin, feeling coherent and capable, like a person who ran errands in the world. Then she stepped outside into the heat.

Halfway home she passed Darius's house, and Darius was on the porch with a fan and a glass of lemonade, waving her up. "Come see what my brother built in the garage," he said. Jade wanted to. The garage had a working model windmill in it. But she stood at the bottom of the steps holding the grocery bag and evaluated the situation instead of climbing them. The milk was cool now, but the day had to be over 32 degrees, and Darius's windmill demos ran long. She remembered the cooler door sign exactly. An hour in this heat, and the milk would be done.

"I can't stop," Jade said. "Not with the milk. Above 32 degrees Celsius, it's only got an hour, and I've already used up some of it walking." Darius blinked at her. "That's a real rule?" "It's on the cooler at the store," Jade said. "Two hours normally. One hour in this heat." She started walking backward down his steps. "Show me the windmill Saturday. I'll bring my own lemonade." Then she turned and jogged, the bag swinging against her knee, the change still jingling in her pocket.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Upstage is the back of the stage, farthest from the audience, and downstage is the front, nearest the audience.
story:
Mia had been in the music classroom three times a week since September, but tonight the risers had been pushed to the walls and the stage felt like a different country. Rows of folding chairs faced the microphone. A strip of blue tape ran along the floor near the edge, and behind it the wood was scuffed and pale, as if a hundred years of shoes had worn a path there. She wondered why anyone would mark a line nobody was allowed to cross, since the rules of the concert already prohibited gum, phones, and talking between songs. Why tape the floor too?

"Places in five," Gurleen whispered, tightening her bow on her violin. "Second row, remember. Between me and Poppy."

Poppy was already standing in the second row, but she had drifted backward while practicing, the way she always did when she was nervous, her heels creeping away from the audience one inch at a time. By the time the lights came up, she was nearly at the back curtain, and the choir's triangle shape had a hole in the middle of it. Ms. Murphy, directing from the piano, caught Mia's eye and tipped her chin toward Poppy, quick and small, so only Mia would see.

Mia thought about the tape again. In drama club, Gurleen had once said something odd: "Upstage is the back of the stage, farthest from the audience, and downstage is the front." Mia hadn't believed her at first, because up should mean higher, shouldn't it? But standing here she could see it was true in the way that mattered. Poppy had gone upstage, and now she was behind everyone, half hidden by the altos in front of her. If Mia pulled her forward, downstage, she'd be back in her spot.

Between verses, when the sopranos took over, Mia stepped back as if to fix her music folder. "Psst. Poppy. You've gone upstage. Come downstage, toward the tape." She held out her elbow, and Poppy grabbed it and let herself be towed forward, blushing, until her shoes touched the worn wood just behind the blue line. The triangle closed up. The hole disappeared.

After the last song, a quiet piece about caribou crossing the frozen tundra, the applause came like rain starting. Poppy found Mia by the instrument shelves.

"You knew the word for it," Poppy said. "Upstage. Downstage. Where did you learn that?"

"Gurleen. Drama club." Mia looked down at the old tape, half peeled, probably obsolete since before their parents were born, and still doing its one job perfectly. "Want to find out who put it there?"

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Hens lay eggs whether or not a rooster is present; without a rooster the eggs are unfertilized and cannot hatch into chicks.
story:
The bus ride out to the farm was long and bumpy, and when they hit the gravel lane the whole back seat went turbulent, so Penelope gripped her notebook and watched the mud puddles by the fence, wondering how long it would take the sun to evaporate them before the class left. On the highway they had stopped at a light right on the median, a strip of grass between the two directions of traffic, and Aaden had claimed he saw a rabbit there, though nobody believed him.

At the farm, Ms. Holloway split them into groups, and Penelope went with Aaden and Susana to the chicken coop. The farmer let them reach under the hens and collect warm brown eggs in a basket. Aaden held his egg up to the light and squinted at it. "There's no rooster anywhere," he said. "I've been looking the whole time. So will these hatch if we keep them warm? Like, could we hatch a chick in class?"

Penelope had been wondering the same thing. She counted the hens, all sixteen of them hopping and pecking, and not one had the long tail feathers or the loud crow she knew roosters had. But there were eggs everywhere, more eggs than she could carry. If the hens needed a rooster to lay eggs at all, there should have been none here. She turned her own egg slowly in her hands, thinking it through. "I don't think they'll hatch," she said finally. "The hens lay eggs no matter what. Without a rooster, the eggs are unfertilized, so there's no chick inside, ever."

Aaden looked doubtful, so Penelope decided to test it. She asked the farmer whether any of these eggs had ever hatched in an incubator, and the farmer shook her head and said, "Not one, and we haven't kept a rooster in ten years." Susana wrote that down in her notebook like a scientist recording proof, and Aaden set his egg carefully back in the basket.

On the way to the goat pen, Penelope kept glancing at the coop and wondering what a fertilized egg would look like from the outside, whether it would look any different at all. "Tomorrow I'm going to candle one," she told Susana. "You hold it up to a light and see what's inside." Susana bumped her shoulder and said, "You're on, but if there's a chick in there, I get to name it."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health

fact: Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
story:
Juliette taped the health-class poster above her desk. It said that mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She read it twice, because Mr. López had said the social part was the one people forgot. She had a reason to check. Lylah had stopped texting her after the argument on Friday, and ever since, Juliette's stomach had been knotting up before dinner and her thoughts ran in circles at bedtime. That was stress, her mom called it, and the knotted stomach was a kind of anxiety.

Juliette formed a hypothesis, the way Mr. López had shown them in science. If the social part of mental health was real, then losing a friendship should change how she felt, and getting it back should change it too. She decided to run a test at home on Saturday. Step one: say nothing to Lylah and record how the morning went. Step two: fix the problem and record the afternoon. She kept a notebook on the kitchen counter and wrote down times.

The morning was bad. Her little brother banged through the kitchen and she snapped at him in an aggressive voice she didn't mean. Her shoulders felt tight, like her whole body had started to contract around the stomachache. At eleven she wrote "no coping, 3 out of 10" and underlined it. Then she called Lylah.

"I set a boundary," Lylah said on the phone. "I'm not doing the apology where you talk and I just stand there. We both talk." Juliette agreed. They made their old ritual, splitting a grilled cheese into exact halves at the counter, and by one o'clock the stomachache had gone and she'd written "7 out of 10" in the notebook. On Sunday she typed a message to Mr. López: "Test worked. Social part counts for a lot." Then she slid the notebook across the counter to her mom, open to both numbers. "Read this," she said.

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused

fact: In credential stuffing, attackers take usernames and passwords leaked from one site and try them automatically on many other sites, so one reused password can unlock several accounts.
story:
Camille's dragon game account had been fine on Friday and empty on Monday, which was why she was glaring at a login screen in the school computer lab instead of eating her pretzels.

"Change your password yet?" Amir asked from the next computer. The lab smelled like warm plastic and the faint lemon of the wipes Mr. Chan used on the keyboards. Somewhere behind the wall, a thermostat ticked as it decided whether the room deserved heat.

"I made a new one. Horsebattery," Camille said.

Amir looked skeptical. "That's it? Two words?"

"It's long," Camille said, and dismissed the little warning box on her screen that said Weak.

Mr. Chan walked past, paused, and kept walking, which was his way of saying think harder.

Camille thought back to Friday afternoon, when her game had still been hers. She remembered a weird email from a website where she'd made an account two years ago to enter one contest for a free kite. The email had said there had been a breach. She'd used the same password there that she used everywhere, because remembering eleven passwords was a job for a wizard. She'd deleted the email and gone back to her dragon.

Now the dragon was gone, and so were her stars, her castle, and her entire sock collection, digital and otherwise.

She turned to Amir. "Okay. Here's my theory. Somebody got the passwords from that kite site, and they tried my same password on other sites, automatically, on lots of them. My game account had the same password, so it opened like a lunchbox."

"That actually has a name," Amir said. "Credential stuffing."

"That sounds disgusting."

"It kind of is."

So Camille tested it. She tried her old password on her bookmark site, her drawing site, and a recipe site she'd visited once. Two of them let her straight in, which meant whoever had the password could get in too. She changed all three, using long jumbles with numbers and symbols, and wrote nothing down that a person could steal, because a sticky note was just a password that walked around asking to be read.

She checked her dragon account one more time. A message sat in the inbox: "Nice socks. Want them back?"

Camille typed, "What socks?" and waited.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

fact: Robert Paine introduced the term 'keystone species' in 1969 for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest.
story:
John had one hour before the science fair, and his food chain poster was still folded like a bad paper airplane in his backpack. He sat in the vet clinic waiting room because his dog, Biscuit, had swallowed a sock, and his mother had said, "Poster comes with us." Kaiden was there too, holding the leash, since his own cat was the reason they'd all become friends with Ms. Sultani, the vet.

"Start with the sun," Kaiden said, peering at the poster. "Sun, grass, rabbit, fox. Done. Nominate me for a medal."

"It's not done. Ms. Sultani said we have to explain what happens if one link disappears." John frowned at his pencil. His problem was that the poster rubric wanted a top predator, and he wasn't sure which animal in his chain counted.

Oakley, waiting with a hamster carrier, leaned over. "Easy. You pull out one thing and everything falls apart. Like at the science museum last month, when you pulled the middle top stone out of the block arch and the whole thing collapsed in front of everybody."

"That was an accident," John said, but he grinned. Then he stopped grinning and started thinking. An arch had a middle stone that mattered way more than it looked. Maybe a food chain had an animal like that too. While Biscuit snored against his knee, John borrowed the clinic's old encyclopedia from the shelf by the fish tank and searched the index.

"Listen to this," he said, and read aloud. "Robert Paine came up with the term keystone species in 1969, for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest." He tapped the page. "Sea stars. There were not that many of them, but take them out and the community reorganizes around the loss."

"Sea stars are foxes now?" said Kaiden.

"Foxes are the top of my chain, but the point is the middle matters too." John drew the sun, then the grass, the rabbit, and the fox, and beneath it he wrote the term in his best block letters, which were consistent in the sense that they were all equally terrible. Kaiden laughed so hard the hamster woke up.

Ms. Sultani appeared in the doorway with Biscuit's diagnosis on a clipboard: one sock, removed, dog fine. "Poster done?" she asked.

John held it up, and Biscuit thumped his tail against the carrier as if he'd drawn it himself.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
story:
Colton stood in aisle three of the pharmacy, holding a green bottle of body wash and reading the back of it twice, because the first time his eyes had slid off the words without taking anything in. His mother had sent him in for her allergy pills, but the basket in his hand also held deodorant, and he was not sure he wanted either item to be his.

He had grown two inches since September. His jeans showed his socks when he sat down, his knees ached at night for no reason he could point to, and last Tuesday, in the middle of answering a question in English, his voice had dropped half an octave and cracked like a dropped plate. He wanted to know what was coming next, and whether he could do anything about it.

A doctor's appointment from the spring came back to him. He had been there for his wrist, which he had bent wrong in gym class, and while the doctor looked at the X-ray on the light board, Colton had asked the question he actually cared about: would he keep getting taller? The doctor had tapped two thin dark lines near the ends of the arm bones on the film. "Bones grow longer at their growth plates, near their ends," she had said. "Once those plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller." Colton had studied the little lines, invisible from outside his skin, and felt both hopeful and impatient. The plates were still open. There was room left.

Now, in the pharmacy, he tried to reason it out. The aching knees had to mean something. He couldn't see the plates any more than he could see inside an egg, but a hidden thing could still leave clues. In science class, Ms. Hamdan had kept a jar on the counter, and the class had learned that a caterpillar larva turns opaque just before it forms its chrysalis, so they had known the change was coming days before it happened. A hidden cause, a visible sign. Maybe the aches preceded the inches, the way the larva's dull shell preceded the change.

He would test it. The doorframe at home had pencil marks on it already, one from every birthday, and he could add a new mark tonight, then another every Friday. If the aches came first and the height followed, he would see the pattern himself.

"Colton? Is that you?" It was Ally from his math class, standing by the register with her little brother, who was trying to reach a candy bar with his whole arm. "You're tall now," she said. "Like, actually tall."

"I'm keeping track," Colton said, and set his basket on the counter. "Every Friday, doorframe, pencil."

Ally squinted at him. "Okay, weirdo." But she was smiling.

At home that evening he stood straight against the doorframe, heels down, and made a small careful mark above the last one. Then he wrote the date beside it and stepped back to look at the ladder of little lines climbing up the wood.

story:
Caleb leaned closer to the screen in the computer lab, where his little cat sprite was supposed to collect coins. Every coin was worth ten points, except one. That one coin, sitting behind the green wall in his maze, was worth two hundred points, and he could not figure out why.

"Did you hide a super coin back there?" Riaan asked, sliding into the chair beside him.

"No. It's a regular coin." Caleb dragged the cat through the maze with his arrow keys and touched the mystery coin. The score jumped. Then it jumped again. Ten points, twenty, thirty, forty, faster and faster, all from one touch. The number climbed past two hundred while both sprites sat there, cat on coin, doing nothing.

"Your game is broken," Riaan said.

"It's not broken. It's doing exactly what I told it." Caleb had made the coin disappear when the cat touched it, but he had forgotten something, and now he wanted to find out what. He decided to decompose the problem, breaking it into pieces the way Ms. Smith had shown them: the forever loop, the if touching block, the change score block, and the part that made sprites move apart. He read them one at a time, top to bottom. The forever loop ran the if touching block over and over. The if touching block added a point. But nothing in his script ever moved the sprites apart.

"So the score keeps going up as long as they touch," Caleb said slowly. "The coin never disappears. That's why it's worth two hundred. It was worth ten points twenty times."

"Twenty times and counting," Riaan said, pointing at the screen, where the score had reached four hundred and ten.

Kara, the computer club ambassador, paused on her way past their row. "Nice venomous snake sprite, by the way," she said, nodding at the bright green snake patrolling the maze wall. "It bit my cat twice at lunch."

Caleb dragged a hide block into the if touching script and clicked the green flag. He steered the cat to the coin, touched it, and the coin vanished. The score ticked up exactly ten points and stopped.

"There," Caleb said. "One coin, ten points. Fair and square."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
story:
Alyssa sat on the porch steps at Kadence's house, staring at the blank card in her lap. Inside, Kadence and Mackenna were laughing at something, and the sound drifted out through the screen door like a door closing on Alyssa alone. Three weeks ago Kadence had been her best friend. Then Kadence had gone to the roller rink with Mackenna on Saturday without even asking her, and after that the two of them walked to school together every day while Alyssa trailed behind.

She had written one line already: "You ditched me at the rink and you know it." She read it again and her stomach tightened. If she gave Kadence that card, Kadence would get defensive and probably write back something just as sharp, and that would be the end of everything. Alyssa tapped her pencil. The problem was the word "you." Every sentence she could think of started with an accusation, and accusations made people argue instead of listen.

She thought about Ms. Ndlovu, who lived next door and sometimes helped her with homework in the garden. Last Tuesday Ms. Ndlovu had been reading a battered old paperback, and when Alyssa asked about it, she had said it was by a psychologist named Thomas Gordon. "He coined the term 'I-message' back in the nineteen sixties," Ms. Ndlovu had told her, holding up the page. "A sentence like 'I felt left out' describes your own feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you.'" Alyssa had nodded politely and forgotten about it until this exact moment on the porch steps.

Now she tested the idea. She crossed out "You ditched me" and wrote, "I felt left out when you went to the rink without me." It was strange how different the same facts sounded. She could almost feel the difference from the outside, the way the first version poked and the second one just opened a window. She decided to test it on paper before she tested it out loud. She wrote a second card as if Kadence were answering: "You always get mad about everything." Even pretending, that one made her jaw clench. Then she wrote: "I felt confused when you stopped walking with me." Her jaw loosened. The pattern held both directions.

She adjusted the ribbon on the card, took a breath that fogged faintly in the cool air, and pushed open the screen door. An ominous gray cloud was building over the rooftops, but she barely glanced at it. Kadence and Mackenna looked up from the kitchen table, where they were making a poster for their math tutor, and the room went quiet.

"I made you something," Alyssa said, holding out the card. "You can read it now, or later."

Kadence opened it right there. Her eyes moved down the page, and then she pulled out the chair beside her. "Sit down," she said. "I didn't know you felt left out. I thought you were mad at me, so I stopped asking."

"I wasn't mad," Alyssa said, sitting. "I was just quiet. There's a difference."

"Then we'd better fix it," Kadence said, sliding a fresh card across the table toward her. "Write one to Mackenna too. She thought you hated her."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Muscle soreness after an unfamiliar workout is usually worst 24 to 72 hours afterward, which is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Grayson finished the first day of basketball tryouts feeling great. His shots had gone in, his passes were sharp, and Mr. Guo had even nodded at him once during the layup drill. On the walk home he texted his friend Kaleb, "Day one crushed. Cuts posted Friday."

He woke up Tuesday and his legs felt strange, heavy, like someone had poured wet sand into his muscles. By the time he reached the stairs at school, he could barely climb them. He found Kaleb leaning against the railing outside the gym.

"You should see me," Kaleb said, wincing as he straightened up. "I thought I was fine yesterday. Now I can hardly sit down."

Grayson tried a jumping jack and stopped halfway through. Tryout day two was Wednesday, and cuts were posted Friday. He needed three more good days, and his legs were getting worse, not better. That did not make sense. Yesterday he had felt fine, and today he could barely move.

At lunch he asked Akram, who had made the team last year, about it. Akram shrugged. "My sister calls it delayed onset muscle soreness. She says after a workout you're not used to, it's usually worst 24 to 72 hours later."

Grayson counted on his fingers. Practice had ended Monday around four. Worst meant Tuesday, Wednesday, maybe into Thursday morning. So the pain should start easing before Friday, but day two of tryouts would land right on the worst of it. He could not skip it, because Mr. Guo was watching cuts, not excuses. But he had one tool left: pacing. If he spent Wednesday's drills at about eighty percent, saving his sore legs for the sprint trial, he might still post a decent time.

Wednesday came, and Grayson followed his plan. He jogged the warmups, took smart shots instead of fancy ones, and told himself not to envy Akram, who bounced around like nothing had happened. During the sprint trial his thighs burned, but they held, and his time was second best in his group.

Thursday morning his legs still ached when he stood up, but by afternoon the stairs felt almost normal again. He checked the gym door after last period. The list was taped up at eye level, and there, third from the top, was his name.

Kaleb appeared beside him, squinting. "Am I on it?"

"Look at row five," Grayson said, and pointed.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
story:
The slushie machine at the Sunoco station had been broken for two days, and Edouard had counted every one of those days. It was the only gas station on the whole road to the lake, a fact so notorious that people planned their bathroom stops around it. Now the machine coughed, sputtered, and dispensed nothing but a sad trickle of blue syrup into a paper cup. The cashier taped a sign to the glass that read LAST ONE, $4, and Edouard stared at it. Slushies were two dollars. He had two dollars.

Outside, his friend Kareem sat at a folding table with a cooler, a bag of ice, and a bottle of blue syrup. "Homemade slushies, four dollars," Kareem announced, scraping the ice with a fork. Edouard tapped his pocket. He had exactly two dollars, which he had planned to allocate between a slushie and a bag of chips. Now it bought nothing. Milan pedaled up on his bike, read the sign on the machine, looked at Kareem's table, and paid four dollars without even blinking. Within an hour, Kareem's cooler was empty and Kareem was walking home with a fat roll of bills.

Edouard thought about that roll of bills all through dinner. If Kareem could charge four dollars because the gas station machine was broken, then anybody with ice and syrup could. The next morning, three tables stood along the road to the lake: Milan's, the twins from Oak Street, and Kareem's again. Each cooler was stuffed full. Edouard rode past slowly, counting, and noticed something odd. Every sign said two dollars now. Some said one fifty.

He pulled up beside Milan. "Why'd everybody drop the price?" Milan shrugged and scraped his ice. "Nobody's buying at four anymore. There's slushies everywhere." Edouard nodded slowly, working it out. Kareem charged a lot, so everybody started selling, and now the road was flooded. "My dad says that's called the law of supply," Milan added, handing a cup to a customer. Edouard dug out his two dollars and bought the biggest blue slushie on the table, which tasted twice as good at half the price. He raised the cup toward the broken machine and said, "Stay broken a while longer."

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: The playwright Harold Pinter wrote 'Pause' and 'Silence' into his stage directions, treating silences as part of what the characters say.
story:
Sebastian stood in the empty auditorium holding his monologue like it might bite him. He had to perform it Friday, and every run-through sounded the same: fast, flat, and forgettable.

"It still intimidates me how big this stage is," he admitted to Aniyah, who was sprawled across the front row seats. Aniyah wanted the drama club's spring showcase spot for herself, so she kept her advice sharp and her eyes on his mistakes.

"The playwright makes it look easy, but your protagonist sounds like he's reading a cereal box," she said. Sebastian scowled and flipped through his script again. That was when he noticed something strange in the old copy Ms. Zhang had lent him from the library shelf. Words sat in the margin where no words should be, printed like tiny lines of their own: Pause. Silence. Pause. He flipped a page. Pause again. "Wait," he said. "This guy Harold Pinter wrote the pauses in. Like they're part of what the character says." Aniyah leaned over to look. "Nobody writes nothing down as a line." But it was right there, ink and everything, as if the silences were being spoken.

Sebastian decided to test it. He ran the monologue again, and at each written pause he stopped completely, three whole seconds, letting his hands hang before the line about the locked door. Aniyah sat up straight. Something in the quiet made the next words land heavier, and Sebastian felt his heart pound like the silence itself was the line. He tried the ending with a long Silence, then a slow turn of his head toward the audience. Aniyah stood and clapped once, loud in the empty hall. "Okay," she said, grabbing her bag, "I'm getting a script with pauses in it too. Give me that copy after Friday." Sebastian grinned and marked the next Pause with his pencil, huge and circled.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
