fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
story:
Mr. Greco had pinned seven old posters above the chalkboard, and Hayden's vocabulary homework sat forgotten in his bag. His real problem was the history fair: he needed a topic by Friday, and every idea he'd pitched had bounced. "Mine? Ads from the 1950s," Naya said, tapping a poster of a beaming family in an affluent suburb holding cereal boxes. "Everybody's buying it," the poster shouted, "join the crowd!" "That's bandwagon," Bilal said. "My sister learned it in debate. They make you feel like a loser if you're the only one not doing something." Hayden squinted at another poster, where a movie star grinned over a bottle of shampoo. "And that one's just a famous person saying buy it." "Celebrity testimonial," Bilal said, sounding pleased with himself.

Mr. Greco wandered by, pretending not to listen, which was his way of listening. "Find a word for the fair," he said, "and follow it around." That night, Hayden's assignment was to look up word histories, and there it was. Propaganda. He read the entry twice, then called Naya, holding his phone awkwardly against his shoulder. "Guess where it comes from. A Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622." "No way," Naya said. "Propaganda started as church business?" "That's the whole fact," Hayden said. "Some pope's committee, four hundred years ago, and now we use the word for shampoo posters."

The next day they tested it. If a committee meant to spread the faith gave the word its start, then the posters weren't random noise; they were organized pushes, using the same tricks again and again. Hayden made a checklist and the three of them went down the row. Loaded words? "Danger! Crisis! Hurry!" Naya counted four. Bandwagon? Six. Celebrity testimonial? Bilal found a poster where the celebrity was a cartoon bear, which they counted anyway, since the bear was technically famous.

At the fair, Mr. Greco stopped at their table, read their poster, and modified his usual frown into something closer to a smile. "You even caught the one with the bear," he said. He pointed to their last line, about how ads can strengthen a stereotype by showing only one kind of person, over and over. "Careful work, all three of you." Bilal whispered, "He said careful. Write that down, Hayden." Naya held out the marker. "Write it in loaded words."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password on its own is not enough to log in.
story:
Brielle sat cross-legged on Jonah's bedroom floor, watching him type his password into the gaming laptop for the third time that afternoon. She could smell the buttery leftovers of the popcorn they'd burned earlier, and outside the window the late sun turned the trees a luminous gold.

"Wait," she said. "Is that the same password you use for everything?"

Jonah shrugged. "It's my dog's name and my birthday. Easy to remember."

Brielle remembered last spring, when her own account had been broken into. She had used the same word for her email, her game login, and the library site, and when someone figured it out, they got into all three. Her mom had made her sit at the kitchen table that night, fixing each account one by one while the dinner dishes went unwashed. "I cherish that memory," she said now, "in the worst way. Let's make you a real password."

They got to work. She had him pick three random words that didn't connect to his life, add capitals and a symbol, and write it on a paper card he'd keep in a drawer, not in his phone. Jonah typed the new password in twice, squinting at the keyboard. "Feels like the frontier up here," he said, tapping his head. "Uncharted."

Then the laptop buzzed and a red box filled the screen. Someone was trying to log into his account right then, from another country. Brielle's stomach dropped, but before either of them could panic, the screen asked for a code that had been sent to Jonah's phone.

"That's two-factor authentication," Jonah said, reading the box out loud. "It asks for a second proof, like a code sent to your phone." He frowned at the message on his screen. "So even if they have my password, they can't get in without the code."

"So the password alone isn't enough," Brielle said slowly. "They stole your old one, but they're stuck." She tested the idea in her head: one password stolen, three doors open. But one second proof, and the door held shut.

Jonah typed the code that belonged to him, changed his recovery email too, and logged out. He picked up the paper card from the desk and slid it into the drawer like it was something worth guarding.

Brielle pulled out her phone and started changing her own passwords, one account at a time, while the room grew dim around them. "Spellchecker37!Maple," she muttered, typing. "Okay. Next."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: A single councillor cannot change a bylaw alone; a change needs a majority vote of the whole council.
story:
Clara had a problem, and the problem had a name: the rink schedule. The outdoor rink behind her school was lit until eight o'clock every night except Saturdays, when the lights went dark at five, which excluded her and every other kid whose parents wanted them home for dinner. Her dad said the schedule was a bylaw, which meant the town council had voted on it, and voting on it meant it could be voted on again. Clara decided that was exactly what she would get done, and she would do it by Saturday.

She wrote to her councillor, Ms. Okonkwo, who everyone said was the most influential person on the council for their part of town. Clara kept the letter short and kept her gloves on, because the thermostat in the kitchen had been stuck at sixteen degrees since Tuesday.

Dear Ms. Okonkwo, my name is Clara and I am eleven. The rink lights go off at five on Saturdays. This is the worst day for us because school lets out at three. Please change the bylaw so we can skate until eight. My friend Romie is helping me collect names.

She got twenty-three signatures in two days, mostly from kids, plus Romie's grandmother and the crossing guard. Then a thick envelope arrived with the town seal on it. Ms. Okonkwo wrote that she was sorry, because she actually agreed with Clara, but she could not just change the rule herself. A single councillor cannot change a bylaw alone; the change needs a majority vote of the whole council.

Clara stared at the sentence until it stopped being disappointing and turned into a clue. If one friendly vote was not enough, then the job was not to convince Ms. Okonkwo. The job was to convince most of the council, which meant more letters, and Romie, who wanted her name on the petition in the biggest handwriting possible, flipped the page over and started a second list. "Twenty-four," Romie said, and clicked the pen.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Ancient Egyptians divided the year into three seasons based on the Nile: Akhet, the flood; Peret, the growing season; and Shemu, the harvest.
story:
Sebastian sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with a blank poster, two markers, and a problem. Mr. Islam had assigned each student one topic about ancient Egypt, and Sebastian's was the calendar. He had to explain why the Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming, and he had exactly one weekend to figure it out.

"Everyone else gets mummies or hieroglyphics," he muttered, drawing a Nile that came out looking like a wiggly snake. His grandpa shuffled in from the porch, holding his glasses up to the window. "These lenses refract the light wrong," he complained. "The optician says my new prescription will be ready Tuesday, so until then everything looks like soup." He peered at the poster. "What's the wiggly snake?"

"The Nile," Sebastian said. "I'm supposed to build a whole calendar around it, but I don't get it. We have four seasons. Why would they have anything different?"

Grandpa lowered himself into the chair across from Sebastian. "Draw me a year on that river," he said. "Start with the water. What happens to a river like that, year after year?" He tapped the blank space above the wiggly snake with one crooked finger.

Sebastian thought about the documentary he'd watched on Tuesday instead of doing his math homework. "It floods," he said slowly. "Every year, the same time. The water goes over the banks, and then it goes back down." He drew a fat blue blob swallowing his snake, then wrote FLOOD above it in block letters. After the flood drained away, the farmers would have wet, black earth, so he drew little green stalks and wrote GROWING. Then, when everything was ripe, they gathered it in, and he wrote HARVEST.

He sat back and stared at what he'd made. Three blocks, not four. No winter, no autumn, just the river deciding everything. "That's why they built the pyramids," he said, sitting up straight. "When the flood covered the fields, the farmers couldn't farm, so all that labor was sitting there unused, and the pharaoh used it. The Nile even gives them their calendar." He remembered the documentary narrator saying the names, and he printed them carefully under each block: Akhet, the flood. Peret, the growing season. Shemu, the harvest.

"So the pharaoh's calendar was really the river's calendar," Grandpa said.

Sebastian grinned, but then his marker froze. "Grandpa, if the flood failed one year, the soil would be impoverished and everyone would go hungry. The whole country was riding on one river." He looked at his poster, at the fat blue blob that could either feed a nation or starve it, and suddenly the pyramids didn't seem like the point at all. He grabbed his phone and called Youssef, whose topic was the pharaohs. "Ask Mr. Islam if we can present together," Sebastian said. "Your kings and my river are the same story."

"Fine," Youssef said through the speaker, "but only if I get to draw the pyramid."

"Deal," said Sebastian, and uncapped the gold marker.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
story:
The message from Giovanni popped up at 4:32, right when Charles sat down at the computer: "Did you SEE this? Article says the Ravens' pitcher got suspended for cheating, that's why we lost the semifinal." Below it was a link. Charles wanted it to be true. His team, the Hornets, had lost 3-2, and for three days he'd been telling anyone who would listen that the Ravens had to be doing something fishy. He clicked.

The page looked strange. There was no author name, no date, and the headline was in giant red letters with three exclamation marks. Charles scrolled down and found the same sentence repeated twice, word for word. His stomach did an uncomfortable turn. If it were real, wouldn't a real news site have it? He opened the site his mom used for actual news and typed the pitcher's name into the search box. Nothing. He tried the town paper. Nothing there either.

He typed back: "Where did you find this?" Giovanni answered fast. "Somebody in our group chat posted it. It sounds right though, doesn't it? They beat us and their pitcher IS exceptional, nobody's that good." Charles leaned back. Here was the odd thing, a kind of paradox: Giovanni believed it because it matched what he already thought, and so did Charles, and neither of them had checked even one word. Charles had practically wanted to accuse the whole team. He'd never once asked whether the story was even real.

He messaged Sofie, the one person he trusted to be stubborn about facts. Her reply came as a short letter in the chat: "Dear doubters. I checked the league's official page. No suspension listed. I also found the game stats. Their pitcher threw 61 pitches, all legal. Somebody made this up because losing feels bad. Ask me how I know. Sincerely, Sofie." Then, a second bubble: "My brother says there's a name for this, confirmation bias." Charles read it twice.

The next morning he showed Ms. Sutton the fake article before class. She looked it over, nodded, and said the site had been reported twice already that week. At lunch Giovanni dropped into the seat across from him, ears a little pink. "Okay, so I shared something dumb." "We both wanted it to be true," Charles said, and slid his tray over to make room. "Rematch is in April. We'll beat them for real." Giovanni picked up his fork and grinned. "Sixty-one pitches, all legal. I'm still going to hit one out."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
The sealed envelope sat on Hudson's desk like something ominous, and it had been there since first period, because Ms. Katz had said whoever it was for could open it later, after the spelling bee. Hudson recognized Chanel's looping handwriting. She was two rows over, chewing her pencil and not looking at him, which meant she was thinking hard about something.

"Order, spellers," Ms. Katz said. "Hudson, you're first. Please come to the front."

His heart started pounding before he even stood up, thudding against his ribs, and his breathing went quick and shallow. Nothing dangerous was happening. It was a spelling bee, not a bear. At recess, Anastasia had mentioned something called fight-or-flight, how when your body thinks there's danger, your adrenal glands release adrenaline, and adrenaline makes your heart beat faster and your breathing speed up. Hudson had half listened. Now he wondered if that was the hidden cause, his body acting like a lion had walked into the classroom when it was only a word list. So he tested it. He took the longest breath he could, let it out slow, and told his adrenal glands, silently, that there was no lion. His heart didn't stop pounding, exactly, but it slowed enough that he could hear again.

"Catapult," Ms. Katz said.

"C-A-T-A-P-U-L-T. Catapult."

"Correct."

When he sat down, he opened Chanel's letter under the desk. I want to enroll in the Saturday art class, it read, but I told my grandmother I'd help at her shop, and that feels like an obligation I can't break. You always say what you're feeling. How do you do it? My stress gets so loud I can't hear my own choices. P.S. You looked green up there. I mean that kindly.

He passed back a torn scrap: My heart was pounding like I was being chased. Turns out that's just what bodies do, not proof something's wrong. Want to talk at lunch? And about the shop, maybe your grandmother would trade you a different morning.

At lunch Chanel set her tray down across from his. "I asked her," she said. "She laughed and said Saturdays were her idea of torture anyway, and to go draw something." She pulled the letter from her pocket, folded into a tiny square, and smoothed it flat on the table between them. "Now tell me the lion thing again, slowly."

Hudson picked up his milk and started from the beginning.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
The whole fight had started in the cafeteria on Tuesday, and Avery replayed it while standing on Lisa's porch. Lisa had walked past the table, and Avery's tray had gone flying, spaghetti everywhere. Avery had said, "You did that on purpose," and Lisa had gone red and said, "Fine, think whatever you want," and they hadn't spoken since.

Karissa had dragged her here. "You two have been best friends since kindergarten," Karissa said, ringing the doorbell. "I miss you both. Also my mom won't drive me home until I fix this, so please comply and just talk to her."

Lisa opened the door with a chewed lip. "What."

"I came to figure out what actually happened," Avery said. "Not to yell." She was being systematic about it, the way Mr. Kovalenko had taught them during the science unit: don't jump to the answer, check the evidence. She thought about that Wednesday in class, when Karissa had raised her hand after Mr. Kovalenko mentioned their psychology reading. "Hostile attribution bias," Karissa had said. "It's when you assume someone meant to hurt you, even though it could've been an accident." Avery had slid lower in her seat, because it sounded way too familiar.

Now she asked, "Where exactly were you standing when my tray went over?"

Lisa led her to the cafeteria after school, since it was still open for basketball practice. She stopped by the serving line and pointed at the floor. A puddle of grease shined near the salad station, half wiped up. "I slipped right there," Lisa said. "My arm flew out and hit your tray. I was carrying napkins because my hands were greasy. I was going to sit with you."

Avery crouched and touched the spot. Her fingers slid.

"Karissa says you won't even look at the group chat," Lisa said quietly. "I kept sending you pictures of the dog I'm trying to convince my mom to adopt. I wanted you to help me name him."

"I'm sorry I said it was on purpose," Avery said. "That was hostile whatever-it's-called. For the record, we should name him Noodle."

Lisa grinned. "Noodle. Okay. Come on, Karissa's waiting, and I saved you the last brownie from home economics."

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: Contour lines spaced evenly apart show a slope that has the same steepness all the way along it.
story:
Kaitlyn spread the topographic map across the library table and pinned the corners down with four paperbacks. "The steepest slope is where the lines crowd together," she said. "Cedric wants to build a jump on the hill behind the school, and if the slope suddenly gets steeper halfway down, the jump will launch him wrong."

Oskar leaned over the map, the little propeller on his winter hat spinning from the force of his breath. He had begged to come along because he wanted the fastest run of anyone this winter, and fast meant steep. "There," he said, tapping a spot where the brown lines bunched tight as piano keys. "That's our hill."

"That's only part of the hill," Kaitlyn said. She traced the lines downhill with her finger, and the lines gradually spread apart, wider and wider, until they were scattered like lazy hoops. "It starts steep, then it flattens out. You'd rocket down the top and then just drift."

"So find a hill where the spacing stays the same," Oskar said.

Kaitlyn had been thinking exactly that. If the lines were packed close and stayed close the whole way down, the slope would keep the same steepness from top to bottom. She slid her finger across the map, hill by hill, hunting for even spacing. Behind her, Cedric was already sketching ramp designs on scrap paper, but without the right hill, his jump was nothing but a drawing.

"Wait." She stopped on a slope west of the creek. The lines there ran close together, and they stayed close, evenly spaced from the summit clear down to the flat ground. "Look at this. Same gap between every line, top to bottom."

"That whole run is steep the entire way?" Cedric left his sketch and hurried over.

"That's what it means," Kaitlyn said. "Evenly spaced lines, same steepness all along."

Oskar spun the propeller on his hat and grinned. Her love of maps was practically hereditary, her dad kept old trail maps in the glove box, and for once it was good for something. She folded the map along the creek line and held it up like a trophy.

"Saturday," Cedric said. "Ramp first, then runs."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The group chat lit up at 4:32 on Tuesday afternoon, which meant someone had a problem.

MIKAELLA: emergency. my grandpa signed my birthday card "Kovács Sandor" but his name is Sandor Kovács. is he ok. do I need to call my mom

Mia stared at her phone. She had seen Mr. Kovács at pickup once, a tall man who called Mikaella "little cabbage," which Mikaella claimed was a compliment. Mia tried to diagnose the situation like her science teacher taught: observe, then make a guess. Observation one: the man was old. Observation two: old people sometimes did things differently. Conclusion: either he was confused, or he was doing it on purpose, and one of those could be tested.

EPHRAIM: my grandpa signs everything with just the letter R. nobody knows why

MIKAELLA: that's not helpful ephraim

EPHRAIM: you're welcome

Mia pulled up the class contact list, where Ms. Dela Cruz had printed everyone's names, and found the three kids from her class whose families had come from China, Japan and Korea. Lin Wei. Tanaka Rika. Park Ji-hoon. She scrolled through the chat history until she found the beginning-of-year introductions, because Ms. Dela Cruz had made everyone share one fact about their name. Wei had written: "In Chinese, my family name comes first, so I'm Wei of the family Lin." Rika had said the same thing about Japanese. Ji-hoon had typed a long message about it and somehow also mentioned perpendicular parking, which nobody had asked about.

Her heart beat faster. Three languages, same order. Could Hungarian be a fourth?

MIAELLA: mikaella. don't call your mom yet. does your grandpa speak Hungarian at home

MIKAELLA: he basically ONLY speaks hungarian. he told my dad the wifi password is in hungarian so no one can steal it

MIAELLA: I think hungarian names go family name first. like chinese, japanese and korean names. like how wei and ji-hoon and rika wrote theirs

There was a long pause. Three dots appeared and disappeared, like Mikaella was typing and erasing, typing and erasing.

MIKAELLA: he retired last year and collects his pension and sits by the window doing crosswords. he is NOT confused. I owe him an apology for what I was about to think

EPHRAIM: tell him the wifi thing worked, nobody has stolen it

MIAELLA: I'm going to write him a note and sign it with MY family name first. Vásquez Mikaella. he'll know I learned something

The next morning a photo appeared in the chat. It showed a sticky note in careful old-man handwriting, leaning slightly like the lines were not quite perpendicular to the page's edge: "Jó reggelt, Vásquez Mikaella. Your grandpa salutes you." Below it, in smaller letters, he had drawn what was unmistakably a cabbage wearing a crown.

"He put my family name first AND made me royalty," Mikaella wrote. "Best grandpa on the entire internet."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Chicago's Engine Company 21 is widely credited with the first fire pole, installed in 1878 after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than others could take the stairs.
story:
The science center's newest exhibit was a real fire pole, polished steel rising two floors into a mock station, and Alexia stood in front of it with her clipboard, trying to figure out one thing: why would anyone put a pole in a building that already had stairs? Ms. Rodríguez had given each group a mystery card, and hers read, "This pole comes from a real question firefighters asked themselves long ago. What was it?" Louise wanted to climb the pole immediately. Oceanne wanted to find the snack bar.

"Look at where they put it," Alexia said, walking a slow circle around the base. The pole dropped straight through a hole in the ceiling, right beside a narrow staircase. "If you had to get downstairs in a hurry, which is faster, going around and down steps, or sliding?" Louise gripped the pole. "Sliding. Obviously. Like at the playground." "But that's a guess," Alexia said. "We need to test it." Oceanne checked her watch while Louise took the stairs, counting the seconds aloud, her sneakers clattering. Then Louise came back up and slid down the pole, and the pole won by a whole count of four.

"So somebody figured that out ages ago," Oceanne said, chewing the edge of her pen. That was when Alexia spotted the brass plaque half hidden behind the exhibit wall. It told about a fire station in Chicago, Engine Company 21, where a firefighter had slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs, way back in 1878, and after that the station put in the first fire pole. "Chicago," Alexia read aloud. "Eighteen seventy-eight. It really was about speed." She copied the words onto her clipboard before the noise of the crowd could dissolve them from her memory.

When the groups gathered to present, a firefighter in full gear asked the class to guess why stations once had poles instead of stairs. Hands shot up around her. "It's from Engine Company 21," Alexia said. "In 1878. A firefighter slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs, so the station put one in." The firefighter grinned and called it the best answer of the day.

Afterward Ms. Rodríguez asked each group to write one critique of their own investigation. Alexia wrote, "We tested with one person, twice. Next time, three people, five tries each." Louise was already back at the pole, and near the entrance a molten-orange sunset poured through the tall windows, sliding down the glass the way Louise slid down the steel. "Last climb before the bus!" Louise shouted, and Alexia ran to join her.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: On Buddhist observance days called uposatha, devout lay Buddhists may take eight precepts, including not eating after midday.
story:
The community hall smelled of incense and old coffee, and Muhammad's stomach had been growling since the ride over. His grandmother had woken him before sunrise for rice porridge, and now it was past one o'clock and the folding tables along the wall held nothing but fruit that nobody was touching. He elbowed Chace, who had come along because his own soccer practice was rained out. "Why isn't anyone eating? There's a whole plate of mangoes."

Chace shrugged. "Maybe they're saving it for later."

Muhammad wasn't sure that was it. He watched the adults instead. Mr. Phan, who owned the building and was the temple group's landlord, sat near the front with his hands folded, and he hadn't touched the fruit either. Neither had Muhammad's grandmother, who normally would have cut him a second helping of everything by now. He tried to quantify the strangeness in his head: one whole afternoon, dozens of people, zero snacks. That was not saving food for later. That was a rule.

He asked his grandmother quietly, and her answer came out vague, something about it being a special Saturday, so he went looking for better data. In the back room, Morgan from his class was stacking cushions, because Morgan's mother helped run the hall and Morgan got dragged to everything too.

"It's called uposatha," Morgan said, nudging a cushion into place. "My mom says on these days people here take eight precepts, and one of them is not eating after midday." Muhammad asked what the other seven were, but Morgan was already carrying a stack of chairs away and just waved a hand like the answer was somewhere in the pile.

Eight precepts. Muhammad stood in the doorway and counted what he could see: nobody eating, nobody arguing, the old radio in the corner switched off instead of playing the usual news. It was like a whole day with the volume turned down. Last summer he had complained through an entire fast day at his aunt's house until his father took him home early, and he still wasn't sure whether he'd been wrong to complain or just wrong to complain that loudly. There had been mangoes that day too, untouched on a blue plate, and he remembered wanting one so much his jaw ached.

His stomach growled again, loud enough that Morgan laughed from across the room. Muhammad walked back to the main hall, sat down beside his grandmother, and folded his hands the way Mr. Phan had done. The mangoes stayed on the table, golden and completely still, all the way until sunset. "Two more hours," Muhammad whispered, and his grandmother smiled and handed him a glass of water.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
The notification buzzed at 7:04 p.m., and Aubrey opened the group chat to find seventeen messages from Harris. "I did it again," the first one said. "I asked to present on Thursday instead of tomorrow. Mr. Choi said okay." Aubrey scrolled up. In September, Harris had volunteered to go first with his weather report. In October he had asked for a one-day delay. In November, three days. Now it was January, and he was pushing his volcano project back a whole week.

"Each one feels worse," Harris typed. "The weather report was just nerves. This one feels like actual anxiety, like my whole chest is tight." Joanna sent a thumbs-up and wrote, "That makes sense, presentations are stressful." Aubrey frowned at her screen. Something about the pattern bothered her. Joanna was being kind, but kindness wasn't the same as an answer.

She typed slowly, thinking it through. "Can I try an inference? The more you push it back, the scarier it gets, right?" "Yeah," Harris answered. "Because tomorrow is scarier than yesterday would have been." Aubrey sat up straight on her bed. That was the clue. Postponing gave him quick relief, she could almost feel how good that must feel, the deadline sliding away like a weight off a shelf. But if the relief was real, the fear should shrink too. Instead it grew. Which meant the skipping itself was feeding it. She asked Harris to elaborate on one thing: "When you delayed the weather report, did the next one feel easier or harder?" "Harder," he said. "Definitely harder."

"Okay," Aubrey wrote. "New coping plan. Tomorrow you present, and I'll stand by the whiteboard and hold up the map of the ring of fire you made, so you're not up there alone. And after, we get dumplings." Joanna added, "I'll hold the vinegar AND the remote for the lava video. Teamwork." "Boundaries though," Harris replied. "Nobody claps extra loud. Just normal clapping." Aubrey laughed out loud and typed, "Normal clapping only, I promise."

The next afternoon Aubrey stood by the whiteboard with the map, and Harris talked for four minutes about Krakatoa, and his volcano erupted baking soda all over Mr. Choi's desk, which was not in the plan but made even Mr. Choi laugh. In the chat that night Harris wrote, "That was still stress. But it was the kind you survive." Aubrey stared at the sentence for a long moment, then closed the thread without typing, because her own swimming test was Friday, and she had been quietly skipping practice for two weeks, telling herself the pool was too cold.

"Mom," she called down the hall, grabbing her towel, "can you drive me to the pool tomorrow morning before school?"

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: On eye prescriptions, OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister.
story:
Norah sat in the waiting area of the optical shop at the mall, holding her new prescription like it might bite her. Across from her, her classmate Hargun was squinting at his own slip of paper with a look of pure dread.

"What's OD stand for?" he whispered. "Because my dad's report from the hospital had letters like that, and it turned out he needed an antibiotic for a week. I think it's a code for optical disease."

"Mine just says blurry at distance," Norah said, which was what the optometrist had told her out loud. But the paper itself was all numbers and those two mystery letters, OD and OS, each followed by minus signs that looked suspiciously like grades.

"We should evaluate this before we panic," she said. Hargun nodded solemnly, as if they were scientists and not two kids waiting for glasses.

The optometrist walked past, and Norah noticed the exam room door still open, the letter chart hanging inside. She stood up. "Come on. We're testing something."

She stopped Hargun at the doorway. "Cover your left eye. Read the chart." He read down to the middle line. "Now the right." He got one line further. Then she pointed at the wall, where a faded poster of an eye diagram was pinned beside a shelf of elastic headbands for sports goggles. The diagram's right eye was labeled with two words in small print: oculus dexter. The left one said oculus sinister.

"Latin," Norah said. "So OD means the right eye. OS is the left one."

Hargun blinked at her. "Right eye?"

"There's no disease. Watch." She pointed to the exam chair, where the optometrist's assistant was entering numbers into the computer. On the screen, the row labeled OD matched what she'd just watched them test first on Hargun, and she'd gone second last week, right eye first, same order. The letters were just directions. Each line told the lens maker which eye needed which amount of blur fixed.

Hargun's shoulders came down about three inches. "So my OD isn't sick. It's just my right eye being its normal wrong self."

"Exactly. Your right eye is slightly worse. Now you know which one to blame."

When Norah's name was called, she went to the frames wall and picked a blue pair, holding them up for Hargun. "Trendy or too much?"

"Trendy," he said. "And if you can see the menu board at the food court with those, I'm buying you a pretzel."

Forty minutes later, glasses on, Norah stood at the rail above the food court and read the smallest line at the very top of the board, the one in tiny print that said ask about our seasonal flavors.

"Pretzel," she said. "And Hargun, your right eye owes me one."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: When ecologist Robert Paine removed a starfish that ate mussels from a stretch of Washington State shore, mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species.
story:
Alexis stared at the blank worksheet in the science lab, where the first line began with a sun and the last box was supposed to hold a top predator. Ms. Sato had drawn arrows on the board from sun to grass to rabbit to hawk, but she had left one question at the bottom: What happens if you remove one link?

"Easy," said Elie, tapping his pencil. "You just cross it out."

Alexis wasn't sure it was that easy. He remembered last summer at a tide pool in Washington State, crouching on wet rocks while an ecologist gently lifted a starfish off a boulder and carried it away. "That's the fifth one from this stretch of shore," the ecologist had said, and Alexis had asked why she was taking them. She only told him to come back and watch the rocks. So he had, the next morning and the morning after that, and the mussels, which the starfish ate, had spread and spread until they covered the rocks and crowded out the crabs and anemones and everything else that used to live there. One predator gone, and the whole shore changed.

"I don't think you can just cross it out," Alexis said. He pulled out a scrap of paper and wrote a quick chain: sun, plankton, mussels, starfish. "Watch. If I erase the starfish, the mussels have nothing eating them." He drew tiny hatch marks over the mussels, then drew little x's through the crabs and barnacles. "That's what I saw at the beach. Mussels took over and the other animals couldn't live there anymore."

Emilia leaned over, eyes wide. "So one arrow can break the whole chain?"

Alexis tested it on his worksheet, erasing the rabbit from the chain on the board. "Then the hawk goes hungry, or the grass gets eaten down differently. But the starfish was worse, because it was the top predator. Take that away and everything below it goes wild."

Ms. Sato walked between the lab benches and paused at their table. "Alexis, would you draw yours on the board? Class, your objective is to explain, in one sentence, what removing a link does."

At the board, Alexis drew the arrows carefully, coordinating his lines so each one touched the next box, then drew a big circle around the mussel explosion. "The starfish was the mechanism holding the shore together," he said. "Remove it, and the mussels crowd everything out."

Emilia raised her hand. "So a top predator isn't just the end of the chain. It's kind of the whole point."

"Exactly," Alexis said, and he drew one last starfish at the top of the board.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast to scratch an itch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining.
story:
The itch started while Rachel was still sitting in the hospital emergency room, waiting for her mom to finish the paperwork. The cast on her broken arm ran from her wrist almost to her elbow, and somewhere under it, invisible and unreachable, something tickled like a fly walking in slow circles.

"Is it bad?" Juliette asked, leaning over from the plastic chair beside her. Juliette had come along because she wanted to see a real emergency room, and she kept craning her neck toward the ambulance doors.

"It's like the itch is hiding," Rachel said. "I can't see it, so I don't know what's causing it." She wondered whether it was one spot or a whole patch, whether it moved or stayed put. If she could figure out the pattern, maybe she could fix it some other way. A ruler stuck out of Subhan's backpack on the floor, and she picked it up, sliding the thin end down inside the cast.

"Stop!" Subhan grabbed the ruler back. He had broken his wrist last year, and he knew things. "The doctor told me the ruler could scrape my skin and wreck the lining inside the cast. The lining is like the soft part, and once it's torn, the cast doesn't protect right."

Rachel pulled her arm back. "Then I'll test something else." She borrowed a straw from Juliette's juice cup and aimed a slow stream of cool air down the side of the cast. Nothing. She tried tapping the outside gently, in a symmetrical rhythm, left side then right side, thinking that maybe pressure on the outside could quiet things deeper in. The itch faded a little, like it was being distracted.

Just then the nurse came by with a boy who was crying, and Rachel heard her say, "That's what happens when you slide a stick in there to scratch." The boy's arm had a raw scrape the doctor would have to look at, and his cast lining was damaged too. Rachel watched him go past, hugging her own cast against her chest.

"What are we going to do about the itch for six whole weeks?" Juliette whispered.

Rachel raised the straw, blew one more puff of air down the cast, and said, "Invent something."

Hailey had read her message to Jakub four times, and it still looked wrong. She had typed "Okay. See you at lunch." after he asked if she wanted to sit together, and he had replied with nothing for a whole math period. In the computer lab, while the rest of the class worked on their state reports, she opened her messages again and stared at the little period after "Okay."

"He's mad," Aniyah whispered from the next computer. "That's what my cousin does. Short answers mean trouble."

"It doesn't say anything mad," Hailey said. "It just says okay." But Aniyah's messages never had periods, and neither did Jakub's, and now that she thought about it, almost nobody used them except her grandmother. She slid her chair closer to Aniyah's screen. "Watch. I'm going to test something." She sent Jakub a new message: "okay see you at lunch." No period, no capital. Then she waited, chewing the end of her pencil, while Ms. Chen walked the rows checking that everyone had saved their work.

The reply came before the bell. "cool!! i'll save you a seat :)" Two exclamation marks and a smiley, which Jakub never wasted on someone he was upset with. Hailey felt something loosen in her chest, but she still didn't understand why one tiny dot had changed everything. Instead of opening her report file, she typed "period at end of text message sincere" into the search bar. The first result made her sit up straight. She read the line out loud, very quietly, so only Aniyah could hear. "A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one."

"So it's not just Jakub," Aniyah said. "Everybody reads it that way."

"Kind of," Hailey said. She thought about the illusion of it, how the words were exactly the same and only the dot was different, and how the dot somehow made the words feel colder even though it didn't say anything at all. It was strange that a mark that small could do so much. She decided to revise her plan for the afternoon, the one where she'd been planning to ask Jakub what was wrong.

At lunch she sat down across from him and slid her phone across the table. On the screen was a message she had written to herself: "Here is what I sent you before." Under it, she had typed it two ways, "Okay." and "okay," side by side. "Which one looks angry?" she asked.

Jakub looked at the screen, then at her. "The first one. Obviously."

"That's what I figured out too," Hailey said, and took a bite of her sandwich. Jakub laughed and stole one of her fries.

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In Lord of the Flies, Piggy's glasses are first used to light the boys' signal fire for rescue, and later Jack's tribe steals them in the night.
story:
Hazel's chart had three columns: chapter, what the glasses did, and what they meant. She had filled the first row weeks ago, when the boys used Piggy's glasses to focus sunlight and light the signal fire on the mountain. "Rescue," she had written in red. Then she'd written it again in chapter five, and again in chapter six, until Lindsay leaned over during silent reading and whispered, "You're just repeating yourself."

"Symbols don't have to change," Hazel said, but the words felt thin even as she said them. Lindsay was out sick the next day, and a folded note came back through the office with the morning announcements. Hazel opened it under her desk. "Still coughing," Lindsay had written in her slanted handwriting. "Did the glasses chart get more interesting, or is it still the word rescue nine times? Because Ms. Pritchard said to track how a symbol condenses everything the boys care about into one object, and I don't think rescue is all they care about anymore." Hazel read it twice, then looked at her chart. Nine times. Lindsay was right, and admitting it stung.

That night she spread the chapters across her bedroom floor like a detective with evidence. The fire the glasses had started was supposed to be a signal, a way home. But when the fire went untended, the boys stopped caring about smoke and started caring about meat. Hazel flipped to the last chapters slowly, almost holding her breath, because she had a guess and she was afraid of it. She found it near the end: Jack's tribe raided the shelter in the dark and stole the glasses. Not the conch, not the food. The glasses. In the first chapters the boys had borrowed them for rescue; now they were taken by force, at night, by boys who no longer wanted to be found.

She tested her idea the way Ms. Pritchard had shown them: she drew an arrow across the chart, from the mountain fire to the raid. One object, two meanings. Sight, then power.

In class the next morning, Kaius argued that the glasses just meant Piggy was smart, which Hazel thought was a biased reading, since he liked Piggy and wanted the symbol to stay kind. "Look at the arrow," she said, turning her chart toward him. "Same glasses. First they light the signal fire for rescue. Then Jack's tribe steals them in the night." Kaius frowned at the paper for a long moment. "So they went from getting everyone saved," he said slowly, "to being loot."

Ms. Pritchard walked past their desks and tapped the corner of the chart once, saying nothing. Hazel added a tenth and final word to the last column, and underlined it twice: control.
